targets.approach: Drive to Ruth Creek Road's end at Hannegan Campground via Mt. Baker Hwy (SR 542) and Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32)/Ruth Creek Road. From the Ruth Creek trail at about 3,450 ft, leave the trail, drop southwest to cross Ruth Creek, and cross talus to the base of the couloir at about 4,000 ft.

targets.descent: Reverse the route with a long series of rappels (double- and single-rope) back down the southeast ramp and west-side benches.

targets.approach: Standard approach is via Holden Village: Lady of the Lake ferry from Chelan or Fields Point Landing to Lucerne, shuttle to Holden, then roughly 8 miles up the Railroad Creek Trail to Lyman Lake. Forest Road 8301 and the Lucerne commercial dock are closed under Forest Service order 06-17-05-26-04, in effect January 28, 2026 through December 31, 2027, after December 2025 storm damage — leaving the longer Phelps Creek Trailhead approach over Spider Gap (roughly 11–12 miles one-way, glacier travel with ice axe required), itself closed through October 31, 2026 by the Little Giant Fire closure (Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-40) and reached only over closed road (Forest Service order 06-17-07-2026-11, through December 31, 2027).
targets.descent_text: Reverse the south-side talus and scree back down to the Lyman Lake basin.

Both options require route-finding through 2006/2015 burn areas with heavy deadfall on the lower trail.

wa_mount_sefrit_southeast_ridge.approach: Drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) to Hannegan Pass Road (FS 32); at 1.3 miles bear left onto Ruth Creek Road and continue to a pullout near milepost 3, just past a creek flowing over a concrete weir (about 2,950 ft), well short of the road's end at Hannegan Campground. From the pullout, cross Ruth Creek (a log crossing has been used) and bushwhack roughly 45 minutes through slide alder and devil's club to the base of the Wall Street couloir.
wa_mount_sefrit_southeast_ridge.descent_text: Reverse the southeast-ridge scramble to the 6,500-ft saddle, re-cross the Northwest Glacier, and plunge-step down the roughly 1,500-ft Wall Street couloir back to the bushwhack and Ruth Creek crossing.
wa_mount_sefrit_southeast_ridge.name: Southeast Ridge

wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.approach: From Glacier, drive Mt. Baker Highway (SR 542) east about 12.5 miles, turn left on Hannegan Pass Road (FR 32), continue just over a mile to the junction with Nooksack Cirque Road (FR 34), and follow FR 34 one mile to its end at the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead (do not confuse with the separate Hannegan Pass Trailhead further up FR 32). Ford Ruth Creek right at the trailhead — there is no bridge, and early-summer high water can make it difficult or unsafe to cross. Follow the old roadbed/Trail #750 up the North Fork Nooksack valley for roughly 50 minutes, then leave the trail and make an ascending traverse onto Sefrit's west/southwest ridge, passing through/around a cliff band, to reach the base of the summit gully system. Above the cliff band, the summit gully splits into several forks; the leftmost fork (or the one just west of a snow couloir to its right) is easiest, and rock is generally solid low but looser near the summit ridge. Note a separate, lower-angle north-side line — via Wall Street Couloir and the Northwest Glacier to the SE ridge — is Class 2 with one exposed ~100 ft Class 3 traverse, and is reportedly the more commonly climbed route on the peak; don't confuse the two l
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.descent_text: Reverse the ascent line: down-climb the Class 4 gully back into the basin, then reverse the ascending traverse to the old logging roadbed and out Trail #750 to the Nooksack Cirque Trailhead. Some parties rappel the short crux step using pre-existing sling anchors rather than down-climb it — inspect any fixed webbing carefully before trusting it, as its age/condition is unknown. Re-ford Ruth Creek at the trailhead; water is typically lowest in early morning, so plan to finish the descent before afternoon snowmelt raises the level.
wa_mount_sefrit_southwest_ridge.name: Southwest Ridge

wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.approach: From Marblemount, drive SR-20 east to the Thornton Lakes Road spur (near milepost 117, just west of Newhalem) and follow the rough, unpaved, high-clearance road about 5 miles to the Thornton Lakes Trailhead (~2,500 ft). Hike the Thornton Lakes Trail — an old logging-road grade for the first ~2 miles, then steeper trail up to the ridge/pass (~4,900 ft) above the lakes — then descend to the lake outlet (~4,400-4,486 ft). Traverse the brushy, sometimes-faint climbers' path around the east/south side of middle Thornton Lake, then climb a long, loose scree/talus gully (roughly 1,200 ft of gain) to a col around 5,750-5,840 ft that serves as the standard bivy site.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, downclimb roughly 30 ft off the north side of the notch to easier rock, then reverse the ridge via a long string of rappels (double-rope where two ropes are carried) interspersed with downclimbing — accounts report anywhere from about 7 to 10 rappels total, including a double-rope rappel off the crux crack pitch — back down to the bivy col. Existing slings and rap rings are present at most stations but the rock is loose, so back up or replace suspect anchors. From the col, reverse the approach gully and climbers' path back around Thornton Lake and out the Thornton Lakes Trail to the trailhead.
wa_mount_triumph_northeast_ridge.name: Northeast Ridge

wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.approach: Approach as for the East Route to Lyman Lake: either from Lake Chelan via Lucerne, Holden Village and the Railroad Creek trail, or from the Chiwawa River side via Phelps Creek, over Spider Gap and down past the Upper Lyman Lakes. Both ways have been closed in recent seasons, the Lucerne side by storm-damaged roads and the Chiwawa side by wildfire and road closures, so check current Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest closures before planning. From Lower Lyman Lake follow Trail #1256 west through forest and meadows to Cloudy Pass (6,440 ft), and gain the ridge crest there to start the traverse.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.descent_text: From the North Star summit, downclimb the summit step, then make a direct beeline across talus toward the Cloudy Pass Trail, intersecting it at about 6,300 ft; follow meadows and interconnected granite slabs roughly 1.5 miles back to Cloudy Pass/Lyman Lake basin.
wa_north_star_mountain_cloudy_peak_trave.name: Cloudy Peak Traverse (South Ridge)

wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.approach: From the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead (end of FR-2150, elev. ~4,600 ft), start on Trail 96 (Snowgrass Flat Trail). The first stretch climbs gently through forest, crossing Goat Creek on a footbridge at about 1.9 miles. Around 2.4-2.6 miles in you'll hear and then reach the springs that form the head of Snowgrass Creek just off the trail to the right - the last reliable, easy water source before treeline. About 0.8 mile past that the trail fords Snowgrass Creek itself; there's no bridge, but logs and rocks usually allow a dry crossing except during heavy snowmelt, when it can run fast enough to require care. Just beyond the ford (~3.9-4 miles, ~5,800 ft) the trail breaks out of forest into the open heather meadows and wildflower bogs of Snowgrass Flat, a scenic rest and water-filter stop before the climb — note that camping is prohibited within Snowgrass Flat itself under Gifford Pinchot wilderness regulations (36 CFR 261.58(e)); parties camp instead at designated sites above/below the flats. Stay left on Trail 96 where the Bypass Trail 97 forks right toward Cispus Basin at about 3.9 miles, and continue straight past the Trail 86 junction (left, to Goat Lake) at about 4.7 miles, stayin
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.descent_text: This is a walk-off, not a technical descent - there is no rappelling on the standard northwest ridge/PCT route. Reverse the ascent line: downclimb the Class 2-3 scramble off the summit block (the loose scree and blocky talus here is the descent crux - go slow, test holds, and stay alert for rock knocked loose by parties above or below you), then pick up the climbers' path back down to the PCT. From the PCT junction, follow the trail back south, again watching footing on any lingering snowfields on the exposed sidehill traverse below the ridge (these are firmest and safest to cross in the morning before they soften). Continue south on the PCT to the Trail 96 junction (~6,400 ft) and descend Trail 96 the way you came - back through Snowgrass Flat, across the Snowgrass Creek ford, past the spring/water source, and down through forest to the Snowgrass Flats Trailhead. No ropes, anchors, or rappel gear are needed for this route under normal summer conditions; a rope and basic glacier/snow travel gear are only warranted for early-season attempts with significant snow cover on the PCT traverse or summit scramble.
wa_old_snowy_mountain_r1.name: Northwest Ridge / PCT approach

wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.approach: From the Dingford Creek Trailhead (end of FR 56, Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road), the fastest approach uses the gated continuation of the road as a mountain-bike/hike-in: roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed (NF-5620) to Hardscrabble Horse Camp near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trailhead, saving significant time over walking it. From there, follow the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River / Dutch Miller Gap Trail (Trail 1030) east along the north bank of the river for several more miles — the tread here is in reasonable shape with minimal blowdown, passing dispersed camps and, in season, overgrown thimbleberry brush that obscures footing on the lower tread. Roughly 13-14 miles in from the trailhead (about a mile before the trail crosses toward Williams Lake/Dutch Miller Gap proper), leave the trail and ford the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River — a real ford, potentially thigh-to-waist deep and cold with snowmelt, so time it for lower water and expect wet feet. On the far side, climb steep, brushy forest into the rocky defile some parties call the 'Valley of the Chiefs,' a roughly two-mile corridor that gains the bench below Overcoat Peak. Continuous snowfields typically begin around 4,600 ft; above
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.descent_text: Reverse the ascent for most parties: from the summit, downclimb the Class 3-4 gully/ledge system on the peak's east side back toward the snow finger and glacier. Where the ledges pinch down at a dihedral feature (a damp, water-streaked corner reported by climbers), most parties do NOT free-downclimb the full corner — instead, build two rappels (roughly full 30m/60m-rope-length pitches) down the dihedral to regain the glacier below. Anchors are natural (slung horns, chockstones, or gear placements) rather than fixed bolts/chains — this is an alpine line with no fixed hardware, so carry a small rack and cordage for anchor-building and expect to leave gear (or plan to down-lead/simul on lower-angle sections to save equipment). A single 60m rope handles both rappels; parties without a 60m would need to break it into more, shorter rappels. Some parties instead find they can downclimb the full gully/ledge system without rappelling if conditions and confidence allow (reversing the ascent by downclimbing is the lower-commitment option), but the two-rappel dihedral descent is the more commonly reported method, especially when the rock is wet or holds are snow-covered. Below the glacier, ret
wa_overcoat_peak_southeast_route.name: East Face

wa_west_face_2.approach: The standard approach is from the Downey Creek Trailhead (off Suiattle River Road) via the southern end of the Ptarmigan Traverse — a rugged, largely off-trail alpine route over Itswoot Ridge/Cub Lake and Bachelor Creek involving glacier travel and significant bushwhacking. Climbers typically budget a full day (or two) of approach before reaching the base of North Peak's granite West Face; this is an experienced-mountaineers-only objective, not a roadside crag.
wa_west_face_2.descent_text: Rappel down the center of the West Face via four consecutive double-rope rappels of roughly 50 m, 50 m, 50 m and 20 m, using natural anchor features and existing bolt/gear anchors established on the granite. Ensure proper rope management to avoid tangling on the steep granite face. Once back at the base of the route, climb back up to the Chikamin-Dome Col via the Chickamin Glacier approach, watching carefully for crevasses and potential moat crossings. From the col, descend the cross-country route back to Bachelor Flats (taking approximately 8-10 hours depending on snow coverage and conditions). From Bachelor Flats, follow the Downey Creek trail back to the trailhead (6-8 hours depending on fitness and pack weight). Plan on getting back to the col the day you climb, then two days out to the car.
wa_west_face_2.name: West Face

wa_beckey_davis.approach: Standard access is via Aasgard Pass into the Core Enchantments: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek and switchbacking up to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft). From the south-end boulder field, climb Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt — the crux of the approach, hazardous under lingering snow into early July with a hidden creek/moat beneath the talus, and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Tranquil and Isolation lakes toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face, roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way. Note that this trailhead/pass can close seasonally (e.g., wildfire closures have forced parties onto the Snow Lakes Trail instead, which one trip report clocked at about 10 miles and 6,000+ ft, roughly 5 hours 44 minutes car-to-base — notably longer and with a different, less direct final approach past Lake Viviane to a climbers' trail on Prusik's south ridge).
wa_beckey_davis.descent_text: From the summit, descend the north face on four single-rope rappels using a single 60m rope, then downclimb 3rd-class ground to the climbers’ path; two optional rappels from stations climber’s right of the gully can replace that downclimb. The first rap station is an old bolt at the true summit (reported to predate the 1980s); the second rappel is built around a wedged block that looks sketchy but has held for decades of parties. Remaining stations are slung natural anchors (webbing/tat) — carry extra material to back up aged slings. From the climbers’ path, scramble around to the base of the West Ridge; some parties report one more short rappel from that notch to regain the south-face base. Total time from summit back to packs is roughly 2 hours in a typical trip report.
wa_beckey_davis.name: Beckey-Davis

wa_boving_christensen.approach: Reached via the same Core Enchantments approach as the other south-face lines: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft), then the south-end boulder field and Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep, loose scree — the approach's crux, hazardous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face, roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country navigation over slabs and talus for the final stretch.
wa_boving_christensen.descent_text: Same north-side descent as the neighboring Solid Gold and Energizer Bunny lines: locate the shared rap anchors on the north side of the ridge and make one full-length rappel (a 60m rope is standard) down to easier ground, then scramble/downclimb roughly 30 minutes back around to the base of the south face. Anchors here are natural (slung blocks/chockstones, webbing/tat) rather than bolted, and per recent forum reports have been periodically rebuilt as old tat accumulates — back up any worn-looking station.
wa_boving_christensen.name: Boving-Christensen

wa_energizer_bunny.approach: Reached via the standard Core Enchantments approach shared by the other south-face lines: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A across Mountaineer Creek to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft), then the south-end boulder field and Aasgard Pass (1.25 mi, ~2,000 ft of steep loose scree — the approach's crux, hazardous under snow into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season). From the 7,841-ft pass, travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn and the base of Prusik's south face — roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,600+ ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country navigation for the final approach.
wa_energizer_bunny.descent_text: Same north-side descent as neighboring Solid Gold and Boving-Christensen: find the shared rap anchors on the north side of the ridge and make one full-length rappel (a 60m rope is standard) to easier ground, then scramble/downclimb roughly 30 minutes back around to the base. Anchors are natural (slung blocks/chockstones, webbing/tat), not bolted, and have reportedly been rebuilt/relocated periodically as old tat accumulates in this area — inspect and back up any worn station.
wa_energizer_bunny.name: Energizer Bunny

wa_preacher_mountain_scramble.approach: Start at the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Trailhead (large lot at the end of FR 56). From the parking area, follow the Middle Fork Trail a short distance and cross the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River on the footbridge, then pick up the Pratt River/Pratt Connector Trail heading west/southwest — an easy, well-graded stretch of roughly 0.6 mile. Watch for the unsigned, unofficial Rainy Creek climbers' path branching off near the Rainy Creek crossing (easy to miss; GPS or a downloaded track helps here since it is not an official maintained trail). This boot path climbs steadily and steeply alongside Rainy Creek, crossing a couple of side streams/seasonal drainages around 3,100 ft — cross here rather than following the valley bottom, then angle south into steadily steepening forest to about 3,600 ft. Around 3,700 ft a short rock band forces a ~100 ft scramble move before you can side-hill in to Rainy Lake (3,800 ft), roughly 3.5-3.75 miles and 2-2.5 hours from the trailhead. The path is boot-trodden, muddy, and brushy in spots (salmonberry/blueberry brush and occasional blowdown), and largely disappears under snow through late spring — expect route-finding by feel/GPS above the lake. Rainy Lake
wa_preacher_mountain_scramble.descent_text: This is a walk-off/scramble-down, not a rappelling route — no fixed anchors or rope work are used on the standard line. Reverse the ascent line exactly: off the summit, follow the ridge north back to the 5,800 ft saddle, then descend north-northwest off the ridge to the small tarn/bench at 5,200 ft, staying well back from any cornice edge if there is snow. From the tarn, drop back down the open slopes and skirt the cliff bands on the lake (west) side of the ridge as before, downclimbing the short rock band around 3,700 ft with care (the single spot on this route with real exposure), then pick up the Rainy Creek climbers' path back down through the brush to the Pratt Connector Trail and out to the Middle Fork Trailhead. Descent time is roughly 3.5-4 hours (about 1.5 hours from summit to Rainy Lake, 2+ hours from the lake back to the car), reflecting the loose talus, brush, and route-finding on the way down being as slow as the way up. Descent-specific hazards: the mossy slab and rock band near 3,700 ft are more consequential to downclimb than to ascend and are the likeliest spot for a slip; the boot path is easy to lose in failing light or fog since it's unofficial and unmarked; and
wa_preacher_mountain_scramble.name: Standard Scramble

wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.approach: Long approach into the Core Enchantments via Aasgard Pass: from the Stuart Lake Trailhead, follow the Stuart Lake Trail 2.5 miles to the Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A junction, cross Mountaineer Creek, and switchback up to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft gain). From the boulder field at the lake's south end, climb Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles gaining roughly 2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt, the approach's physical crux, hazardous under lingering snow (a hidden creek/moat under the talus) into early July and avalanche-prone in shoulder season. From the 7,841-ft pass, continue cross-country through the upper Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Prusik Pass and Gnome Tarn, where parties commonly bivy roughly 20 minutes from the base of Prusik's south face (there is no maintained trail for this last stretch — it's cross-country over slabs and talus). Total is roughly 7.5–8 miles and 4,500+ ft one-way. Overnight camping in the Core Zone requires an Enchantments permit; the Snow Lakes Trail is a longer (9+ mile) alternative when the Stuart/Colchuck trailhead or Aasgard Pass is closed.
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.descent_text: From the summit, rappel the north side on four single-rope rappels with a 60 m rope, then downclimb 3rd-class ground; one or two optional rappels right of the gully replace the downclimb. Anchors mix a bolted station near the top of pitch 1 with gear/piton anchors and slung natural features lower down — carry extra webbing to back up older tat. After the fifth rappel, scramble down to the balanced-rock landmark at the base of the West Ridge and make one additional single rappel to reach easier ground before walking back to the south-face base.
wa_prusik_peak_der_sportsman.name: Der Sportsman

wa_prusik_peak_prayer_for_a_friend.descent_text: Since the route finishes at the top of the headwall rather than the true summit, parties scramble the remaining West Ridge terrain to the summit, then descend via the West Ridge's four-rappel descent.
wa_prusik_peak_prayer_for_a_friend.name: Prayer for a Friend

wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.approach: From the Stuart Lake Trailhead (3,400 ft) at the end of FS Road 7601, follow the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599A) junction. Turn left, cross Mountaineer Creek (a rock-hop/log crossing and the last reliable, easy water source for a while), and switchback up 1.6 miles through forest to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft) — roughly 4.1 miles and 2,000 ft from the car. Boulder-hop along the lake's east shore to the boulder field at its south end (about 5.5 miles in, 2,500 ft gained), then pick up the climbers' trail/talus leading to the base of Aasgard Pass. Aasgard Pass itself gains about 2,000 ft in only 1.25 miles of steep, loose dirt and scree — physically the crux of the approach. It's cairned when snow-free, but in early season (often into July) snow can bridge a hidden creek/moat on the left side of the gully that has caused serious injuries and at least one fatality when climbers post-holed or glissaded into it; the slope is also avalanche-prone with a spring/early-summer snowpack. From the top of the pass (7,841 ft) descend gently into the upper Core basin past Isolation/Tranquil Lake, then continue cross-country roughly 1–1.5 miles north over
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.descent_text: From the top of Solid Gold, most parties continue to easy ground and locate the shared 'Solid Gold' rap anchors (also used to descend Sail Away and other nearby lines) on the north side of the ridge. The standard descent is a single, full-length rappel — a 60m rope is typical — down the north face, landing on easier ground below; from there it's about a 30-minute scramble/downclimb east back around to the notch below the West Ridge and the base of the south face. Some parties instead break this into two shorter rappels from the same general anchor area depending on rope length and party size/gear drag. Anchors are natural (slung blocks/chockstones with webbing/tat), not bolted, and the anchors in this immediate area (shared with the West Ridge descent) have been periodically rebuilt and relocated as old tat accumulates — inspect and back up any station that looks worn.
wa_prusik_peak_solid_gold.name: Solid Gold

wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.approach: Long approach into the Core Enchantments via Aasgard Pass: Stuart Lake Trailhead → Stuart Lake Trail (2.5 mi) → Colchuck Lake Trail #1599A, crossing Mountaineer Creek and switchbacking to Colchuck Lake (5,570 ft, ~4.1 mi/2,000 ft). From the south-end boulder field, ascend Aasgard Pass — 1.25 miles, roughly 2,000 ft of steep, loose scree/dirt, the approach's crux, hazardous under lingering snow into early July (hidden creek/moat beneath the talus) and avalanche-prone in shoulder season. From the pass (7,841 ft), travel cross-country through the Core past Isolation/Tranquil Lake toward Gnome Tarn, then contour below Prusik to the base of the south face and the start of the route — about 7.5–8 miles and 4,600 ft one-way, with unmarked cross-country travel over slabs and talus for the final stretch. Overnight camping in the Core requires an Enchantments permit; a longer Snow Lakes Trail alternative exists when Aasgard Pass or the Stuart/Colchuck trailhead is closed.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.descent_text: Walk east from the summit and begin the north-face rappel line on slung belay stations — natural anchors (blocks/chockstones with webbing/tat); there's little to no fixed gear at the top. Plan on four single-rope rappels of about 25-30 m, then a 3rd-class downclimb; one or two optional rappels right of the gully replace the downclimb. Figure roughly an hour from the summit back to the base if the rap line isn't backed up with other parties, which does happen since several south-face routes share this descent. Bring extra tat to back up aged webbing on the natural anchors.
wa_prusik_peak_south_face_burgner_stanle.name: South Face (Burgner-Stanley)

wa_prusik_peak_taylor_wood_route.descent_text: Two options: descend using the Stanley-Burgner route’s north-face rappel descent, four single-rope rappels then a 3rd-class downclimb, or make about five rappels down the couloir to the right of the route followed by easy scrambling back to the base. A single 60m rope suffices for both the ascent and the rappel descent.
wa_prusik_peak_taylor_wood_route.name: Taylor-Wood Route

wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.approach: Start at the Stuart Lake Trailhead (Trail #1599) at the end of Eightmile Road/FS-7601, elev. ~3,400-3,600 ft. Hike the Stuart Lake Trail about 2.5 miles to the signed junction with the Colchuck Lake Trail (#1599 continues to Stuart Lake; branch left onto the Colchuck Lake Trail). This spur crosses Mountaineer Creek on a footbridge/logs (last reliable, easy water before the basin) and then climbs a rocky, switchbacking 1.6 miles through forest and boulder fields to Colchuck Lake at 5,570 ft (roughly 4.1 miles and ~2,200 ft from the trailhead) - a good rest, filter-water, and gear-sort stop. Skirt the east/south shore of Colchuck Lake on climbers' trail to the large boulder field at its south end, then begin the Aasgard Pass climb: follow the outlet stream/drainage, staying climber's-left of the first band of cliffs, up steep heather, rock steps, and (in early season) snow. This is the approach crux - roughly 2,000-2,200 ft of gain in under a mile on what regulars describe as a 'jenga pile' of loose scree and talus with real fall-and-rockfall consequence; an ice axe (and crampons in early season/on residual snow) is worth carrying into July. wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.descent_text: From the summit, the standard descent drops down the north side of Prusik Peak via a sequence of rappels, then traverses back to Prusik Pass to rejoin the approach line. Most parties make four rappels, then downclimb loose 3rd-class ground; one or two optional extra rappels can replace that downclimb - the first anchor is typically right at your feet on a flat spot at/near the true summit, with subsequent stations found by rappelling roughly 20-30m and looking climber's-left; anchors are fixed gear (slings/webbing 'tat' and rap rings/chains left by parties over the years, not bolted), so back them up or inspect carefully. Rappel lengths run mostly in the 25-30m range with one shorter first pitch; a single 60m rope is adequate for every station for a party of two, though a doubled 60m (30m per strand) can feel tight on the last traverse-y rappel, and parties of three often prefer a 70m rope for margin. After the last rappel, traverse west (skiers'-left) across talus back to Prusik Pass at the base of the West Ridge - this is not a walk-off from the summit itself, but the technical descent is short (well under an hour for an efficient party) and feeds directly back into the approach
wa_prusik_peak_west_ridge.name: West Ridge

wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.approach: Start at the Pacific Crest Trailhead (PCT trailhead) at Snoqualmie Pass West, reached via I-90 Exit 52 — this is the road-access endpoint; from the trailhead the hike itself begins on the newer rerouted Pacific Crest Trail heading north. Follow the PCT for roughly 2–2.5 miles of well-graded, well-maintained trail through old-growth forest with blueberry and salmonberry understory. At the signed junction, leave the PCT and turn left onto Trail #1033, the Commonwealth Creek Trail, following it up Commonwealth Basin toward Red Pass. The trail parallels and crosses Commonwealth Creek in the basin, which is the one reliable natural water source on the approach (treat before drinking) — carry enough water above this point since the final scramble slopes are dry. As the trail levels out near a small tarn/pond below Red Mountain's west slope, watch for a cairn planted in the middle of the path — this marks the scramble takeoff point where you leave the maintained trail. wa_red_mountain_snoqualmie_standard.descent_text: No rope or rappelling is used on the standard route — this is a pure walk/scramble descent. Most parties reverse the ascent line down the west-slope boot path back to the cairn and Commonwealth Creek Trail, then retrace the Commonwealth Creek Trail and PCT back to the trailhead. Some parties instead descend via the southwest ridge crest before dropping back into the boot-path drainage, which can offer more solid footing than the loose central scree the boot path sometimes follows — either line rejoins the same trail system before the pond. The overriding descent hazard is loose, fractured rock underfoot (a helmet is strongly recommended for the whole party, not just the leader, since Red Mountain's red rock is notoriously fractured and easy to kick loose onto climbers below); keep the group tight and avoid spreading out on the open scree. Do not attempt to traverse east/south off the summit toward the PCT near the Kendall Catwalk as a shortcut — that terrain quickly becomes Class 3/4 and cliffs out without a rope. wa_south_face_7.approach: From the PCT trailhead at Exit 52, hike the Pacific Crest Trail north to the Commonwealth Creek Trail junction, then follow it roughly 2 miles until Red Mountain comes into view. Traverse on heather across the base of the mountain until you reach the bright red rock gully/ramp that marks the start of the route.
wa_south_face_7.descent_text: Standard descent follows the class 2 scrambling line on the west side of the south ridge back down. If the party continued up the steep summit block direct, a rappel using tree anchors with webbing and rap rings is an option.
wa_south_face_7.name: South Face
